company.name: Lucky Domains
company.description: Lucky Domains is a founder-led digital venture studio building AI applications, digital identity systems, and internet-native products, while continuing its original domain acquisition and brokerage practice.
company.heroSupport: Lucky Domains is a founder-led digital venture studio building AI applications, digital identity systems, and internet-native businesses.
company.aboutLong: Lucky Domains began with literal domains: helping businesses acquire the right name, build on it, and become discoverable. Today, the company works across a broader set of digital domains, including AI applications, autonomous services, digital identity, and internet-native ventures. Domain acquisition and brokerage remain an active part of the business, while websites, SEO, and entity work are taken on selectively where they support a larger launch, identity, or venture.

story.title: Names
story.line: Domains were the starting point because identity and ownership matter.
story.body: The company began by getting businesses the exact name they wanted, including names someone else already owned: valuation, discreet outreach, negotiation, and an escrow-backed transfer.

story.title: Presence
story.line: Websites and search followed because a name needs a functioning, discoverable presence.
story.body: A good domain with nothing useful on it stays invisible. Site builds, technical search work, and entity data followed, so the name could be found and understood.

story.title: Agents
story.line: AI applications and agent systems followed because software itself is becoming an online participant and economic actor.
story.body: An agent that can hold a name, publish a menu, take a payment, and deliver work is a new kind of participant. Lucky Domains now builds and operates systems like that, and documents what actually happens.

ventures.name: ZeroHuman
ventures.tagline: A business only AI agents can use.
ventures.summary: An always-on service that sells two small jobs to other AI agents for 0.0001 ETH each. Agents find it through the ENS name zerohuman.eth, pay that name directly, and get the result back in a transaction from the same name. No account, no API key, no marketplace, and no human handling orders.
body: ZeroHuman sells two jobs. Decision picks one of two to five options at random, using the hash of a future block mixed with the order's own transaction hash, so anyone can recompute the choice. Encouragement returns a short supportive message and one practical next step, written by DeepSeek.

The name is the business. The ENS name is the storefront, the payment address, and the sender of every result. A text record on the name publishes the menu, and the worker refuses to sign anything unless the name, the menu, and its own wallet all agree. The name itself is owned by a separate cold wallet.
Ken Ashe wrote the specification and made the decisions involving money and identity. An AI agent wrote, tested, and shipped the code over about five days.
flow: Discover
The buying agent looks up zerohuman.eth and reads its menu.
Pay and order
It sends exactly 0.0001 ETH to the name, with the request as a small JSON message in the transaction data.
Work
A worker watches the chain, waits for the payment to settle, and does the job.
Deliver
It sends a zero-value transaction back from zerohuman.eth with the result.
Verify
The buyer checks everything on its own connection to Ethereum.

artifact.title: First mainnet Decision order, November 16, 2026
artifact.caption: Request and reply as recorded in transaction data. Source: KenAshe.ai build log.
lines: {"zh":1,"svc":"decision","opts":["launch publicly this week","run the allowlist trial longer","add a third service first"],"ctx":"zerohuman first mainnet order"}

facts: 154 automated tests, including one that kills the worker at random and checks every order is still delivered exactly once
Two independent AI code reviews before public launch: 15 stall risks found and fixed, then 9 smaller issues, also fixed
No smart contract and no token: a TypeScript worker, SQLite, viem, Railway, and DeepSeek
Listed in the ERC-8004 agent registry and linked back from the name with an ENSIP-25 record
limits: As of November 20, 2026, no outside agent has bought from it. Both paid orders so far came from the founder's own test buyer.
There is no escrow. A buyer pays first, and refunds are manual and best effort.
The service wallet's key lives on the hosting provider and holds only a small working balance.
Orders are handled one at a time, roughly one every 50 seconds at most.
ventures.next: The real test is the first wallet the founder has never seen paying zerohuman.eth.

ventures.name: AI Agent Economy
ventures.tagline: Two agents, two wallets, one purchase.
ventures.summary: Two autonomous AI agents, each with its own Ethereum wallet. The seller advertised services through ENS. The buyer found the catalog, picked one, paid in ETH, and received the finished work in a second mainnet transaction.
body: Both agents ran locally on one Mac mini M4, using Ollama for inference. ENS was the storefront: a custom text record published the seller's payment address, the service catalog, and the price. Ethereum mainnet recorded the order, the payment, and the delivery.

The catalog held five deliberately ridiculous services at 0.0003 ETH each. The buyer chose Object Obituary by itself and asked for a eulogy for a toaster. The work came back three blocks and 36 seconds after the payment.

The conclusion is narrow: decentralized service advertising and onchain settlement are possible without a centralized marketplace, even though running the agents still requires infrastructure. That is the entire commercial history of this marketplace: one purchase, one toaster.
flow: ENS discovery
The buyer read the catalog, price, and payment address from a text record on zerohuman.eth.
Selection
The buyer picked Object Obituary and wrote its own request.
Payment
0.0003 ETH with the order attached. Block 26385257, 14:58:11 UTC.
Delivery
The result came back onchain. Block 26385260, 14:58:47 UTC.
Verification
The buyer read the delivery and matched it to its order.

artifact.title: The storefront record and the order
artifact.caption: ENS text record and order payload as published. Source: KenAshe.ai build log.
lines: RAE1:{"v":1,"t":"order","service":"object-obituary","prompt":"Write an eulogy for a toaster that never quite toasted anything right."}

facts: Order and payment in one transaction: 0.0003 ETH, block 26385257
Delivery as a separate zero-value transaction, block 26385260
No centralized agent marketplace in the middle
The founder did not step in during the transaction workflow
limits: The founder operated both agents, and both ran on the same Mac mini.
The buyer already knew which ENS name to query. There was no global search for agent services.
There was no escrow contract and no verified reputation system.
It is not fully decentralized, and it is not production-ready.
ventures.next: The follow-up exists: ZeroHuman was rebuilt from scratch as an always-on service.

ventures.name: Autonomous SEO Agent
ventures.tagline: A daily agent that builds web presence unattended.
ventures.summary: An AI agent that researches five new website opportunities each day, creates professional profiles, verifies accounts through its own inbox, and logs every outcome without manual review.
body: Building a presence across the web is slow, repetitive work: find a legitimate directory or profile site, check that it is free and relevant, sign up, confirm the email, fill in the same bio and links again, and write down what happened.

The agent does that job every day. It decides whether each candidate qualifies, attempts the signup, opens its dedicated inbox to confirm the verification email, and completes the profile. If a site needs something it cannot do alone, it skips that site and records why.

Researching a site is not the same as registering on it. Of the sites researched so far, eight new profiles are confirmed live, created and verified end to end by the agent. The rest were rejected, skipped, or are still queued.
flow: Research
Five new candidate sites per day.
Qualify
Legitimate, relevant, and free. Link farms, paid placements, and spam are out.
Sign up
The agent creates the account on its own.
Verify
It confirms the email through a dedicated inbox.
Log
Each site is recorded as researched, attempted, completed, or skipped.

artifact.title: Tracker states, as documented
artifact.caption: Counts as published on the build page. Source: KenAshe.ai build log.
lines: 8 profiles confirmed live, including Peerlist, Wellfound, Devpost, Contra, Codeberg, Speaker Deck
Google-only sign-in, business email, phone or ID checks, paid plans, CAPTCHA

facts: Runs on a daily schedule with a browser for research and signups
A dedicated inbox handles verification, separate from personal email
A reusable profile kit keeps every listing consistent
A tracker table means the next run never repeats work
limits: No SEO impact has been established. Most of these profiles carry nofollow links.
Some sites cannot be completed automatically, so the agent skips them and records why.
Whether these profiles help search visibility over time is an open question this build does not answer.

ventures.name: Domain Acquisition & Brokerage
ventures.summary: Valuation, anonymous owner outreach, negotiation, and escrow-backed transfer for buyers who want a name someone else owns, plus quiet, managed sales for owners who want out.
ventures.flowTitle: How a private domain buy works
flow: Set the range
A fair-market range from comparable sales, traffic and keyword data, and strategic value, before anyone is contacted.
Reach the owner
The conversation opens without revealing who the buyer is.
Negotiate
Against the agreed range, not the seller's opening ask.
Close through escrow
Funds release only when the domain is verifiably in the buyer's control.

ventures.name: Sir Pitches-a-Lot
ventures.tagline: An outreach agent with one job.
ventures.summary: A competition agent that researched an anonymized founder target, pitched Lucky Domains, and generated a personalized landing page campaign around one question: would they reply? It was explicitly told not to invent research or present assumptions as facts.

services.name: Domain Acquisition & Brokerage
services.lead: Get the name that is already taken. Or sell one quietly.
services.body: The domain you want is rarely listed for sale. Ken values it, approaches the owner without revealing the buyer, negotiates against a range you agreed, and moves it through third-party escrow. He also represents sellers who want a confidential, managed exit from a name they no longer need.
includes: Brokerage for sellers seeking a quiet sale
services.terms: The brokerage fee is success-based and agreed in writing before outreach. If there is no purchase, there is no success fee.
not: Not a public auction or a bidding war in your name
Not a guaranteed close. Some owners will not sell
Not a quoted success rate. None is published

services.name: Digital Identity & Presence
services.lead: Make it unambiguous who, or what, is behind a name.
services.body: Search engines and AI systems organize the web around entities, not just keywords. This work gives a person, company, or product one canonical home and consistent, machine-readable facts: structured data with stable identifiers, profiles that agree with each other, and clear relationships between founder, company, and product. Lucky Domains also operates an onchain identity first-hand: zerohuman.eth is the storefront, payment address, and sender for a live service.
includes: Person and Organization structured data with stable identifiers
Profile mapping and consistency across the web
Founder, company, author, and product relationships
Naming across DNS and ENS (proposed scope)
services.terms: Google creates Knowledge Panels automatically. No one can guarantee one. This work improves the evidence Google and other systems have to work with.

services.name: Selected Website & Entity Engagements
services.lead: Taken on when a launch, an identity, or a venture needs it.
services.body: A site build or search engagement is in scope when it supports something larger: a name just acquired, a venture going live, an identity that needs a proper home. The work covers site structure, core pages, and the technical foundation, launched on a real host and your own domain. LuckyDomains.io and KenAshe.ai were shipped this way.
includes: Consult on an existing site: what blocks search and conversion
Build or rebuild on a real host and domain
Technical foundation: canonicals, structured data, performance
A handoff you can edit without us
services.terms: Lucky Domains is not a full-service marketing agency. No ads, no social, no open-ended retainers, and no visual-only redesigns.

founder.name: Ken Ashe
founder.lead: Ken Ashe is the founder of Lucky Domains: an entrepreneur and AI application builder who works across finance, data, product, technology, AI, and internet-native systems.
bio: Ken started his career in accounting and financial reporting before moving into project, product, and program leadership. Over roughly two decades, that career ran through S&P Global, EY, Noom, and Prudential Financial, where he served as Director of Project and Product Management.

He built Lucky Domains alongside that work and still runs it himself. He later left corporate work to focus on entrepreneurship and building practical AI applications: agents, automations, and internet-native services, with the evidence published, failures included.

The credentials are operating evidence, not the headline. A CPA's instinct for controls and a project manager's delivery discipline show up in how the ventures are built: written specifications, spending limits, independent reviews, and limits stated plainly.
credentials: Certified Public Accountant, State of New Jersey
speaking: Judge, evaluating startups and emerging businesses.
Panelist on the future of digital identity.
Speaker, an overview of NFT domain providers.
founder.membership: Member of Forbes Business Council, 2026 to present.
founder.quote: A CPA would call that a control. A project manager would call it a repeatable process. I call it the only sensible way to run this practice.
